name: Claude Certified Associate – Foundations
audience: Business professionals, analysts, consultants, and team leads who use Claude every day as a productivity tool. You don't need to code. The exam checks whether you can get reliable work out of Claude, judge its output critically, pick the right product surface, and use it responsibly inside an organization.
format: 60 multiple-choice and multiple-response items in 120 minutes, scored on a 100–1,000 scale with 720 to pass. Delivered by Pearson VUE (online proctored or at a test centre). Multiple-response items tell you how many to select and are scored all-or-nothing. Items are scenario-based: you are a professional with a goal, and you choose the best way to use Claude.

domains.name: Prompting & Task Execution
domains.summary: Writing clear, context-rich prompts. Breaking big tasks into steps. Using examples, structure, and success criteria. Iterating instead of starting over.

domains.name: Output Evaluation & Validation

domains.name: Product & Model Selection
domains.summary: Matching the task to the right Claude surface (web, desktop, mobile, Claude Code, Chrome/Excel integrations), the right model tier (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku), and the right feature (web search, Research, extended thinking, artifacts).

domains.name: Workflow Integration & Solution Design

domains.name: Configuration & Knowledge Management

scenarios.title: Marketing campaign lead
scenarios.description: You run a product launch. You use Claude to draft messaging variants, adapt copy across channels, analyze survey feedback, and keep brand voice consistent with a shared Project and custom style. Watch for factual claims about the product and any competitor comparisons.

scenarios.title: Financial / business analyst
scenarios.description: You upload spreadsheets and reports, ask Claude to summarize trends, build quick analyses, and draft board-ready commentary. Every number has to be traceable, and the calculations have to be verifiable.

scenarios.title: HR policy partner
scenarios.description: You draft and update policies, answer employee FAQs, and summarize regulations. The content is sensitive (personal data, legal exposure), so data handling, accuracy, and human sign-off matter most.

scenarios.title: Sales operations manager
scenarios.description: You connect Claude to the CRM, email, and calendar through connectors, prepare account briefs, and standardize proposal drafts across the team. Your concerns are permissions, consistency, and keeping customer data out of the wrong places.

scenarios.description: You use Claude to draft macro responses, summarize ticket trends, and build a knowledge-base Project for agents. Responses must match policy, avoid made-up commitments, and escalate edge cases to people.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an effective prompt
lessons.summary: Claude does its best work when you treat it like a brilliant new colleague who has zero context. Give it the goal, the audience, the background, the constraints, and what 'good' looks like.

sections.heading: The 'new colleague' mental model
sections.body:
Claude can't see your inbox, your company's history, or the meeting you just left, unless you give it that information or connect a tool that can. A useful test: **would a smart new hire, handed exactly this text, produce what you want?** If not, add context.

Most weak outputs come from weak inputs. A vague request like "write an email about the delay" makes Claude guess the audience, tone, length, cause, and next steps.

sections.heading: The building blocks
sections.body:
A strong prompt usually includes:

- **Task**: what to produce, stated directly ("Draft a 150-word email...").
- **Context**: background, why it matters, who it's for.
- **Role or perspective** (optional): "You are reviewing this as a skeptical CFO."
- **Inputs**: the documents, data, or notes to work from, clearly separated from your instructions.
- **Constraints**: length, format, tone, things to avoid, deadline-driven priorities.
- **Success criteria**: how you'll judge the result ("A non-technical customer should understand it in one read").
- **Examples** (optional but powerful): one to three samples of the style or format you want.

sections.heading: Structure with tags and headings
sections.body:
When a prompt mixes instructions with long material, separate them so Claude doesn't confuse the two. XML-style tags work well:

```
Summarize the customer feedback below for our product team.
Group it into themes, count mentions per theme, and quote one example for each.

<feedback>
...paste survey responses here...
</feedback>
```

Tags like `<document>`, `<notes>`, or `<example>` aren't magic keywords. They're clear labels. Markdown headings work too. What matters is that the boundaries are unambiguous.

sections.heading: Examples (few-shot prompting)
sections.body: Showing beats telling. If you want a particular voice or format, paste one or two examples and say what to copy (tone, length, structure) and what **not** to copy (the specific facts). Use examples that vary a little, so Claude learns the pattern instead of cloning one sample.

sections.heading: Ask for what you want, positively
sections.body: "Write in plain, flowing paragraphs" works better than "Don't use bullet points." Say why a constraint exists ("this will be read aloud, so avoid lists and symbols"). The reason helps Claude handle cases your rule didn't anticipate.

keyPoints: Context is the biggest lever. Assume Claude knows nothing about your situation.
State the task, audience, constraints, and success criteria explicitly.
Separate instructions from source material with tags or headings.
One to three varied examples teach a format or voice faster than adjectives.
Explain the reason behind a constraint so Claude can generalize it.

gotchas.trap: Making the prompt longer with ALL-CAPS warnings and repeated 'MUST' statements.
gotchas.correct: Add clear context and a reason for each constraint. Calm, specific instructions work better than shouting.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Claude remembers details from an unrelated earlier chat.
gotchas.correct: Give the needed context in the current chat, or use a Project or memory deliberately. Never assume it carries over.

gotchas.trap: Pasting a document and writing 'thoughts?'
gotchas.correct: Say what you want: the decision you're making, the angle to review from, and the output format.

lessons.lab: Take a real task from your week (an email, summary, or plan). Write a one-line prompt in claude.ai and save the result. Then rewrite the prompt with task, context, audience, constraints, success criteria, and one example, and compare the two outputs side by side. Note which additions made the biggest difference.

lessons.title: Task decomposition, iteration, and thinking
lessons.summary: Big, fuzzy tasks give generic results. Break the work into stages, review each stage, and refine in the same conversation instead of starting over.

sections.heading: Why decompose?
sections.body:
A prompt like "Write our Q3 strategy deck" bundles research, analysis, structure, and writing into one step. Splitting it gives you a checkpoint after each stage:

- **Step 1:** "Here are our Q3 numbers and goals. List the 5 most important findings, with the data behind each."
- **Step 2:** "Using findings 1, 2, and 4, propose a 7-slide outline."
- **Step 3:** "Draft speaker notes for slides 1–3."

Each step is easier to check, and an error caught early doesn't spread into the final product. This is called **prompt chaining**.

sections.heading: Iterate, don't restart
sections.body:
First drafts are a starting point. Give specific feedback: "Shorter. Lead with the customer benefit. Cut the second paragraph. Keep the call to action." Specific feedback converges faster than "make it better."

When a conversation has gone badly wrong (built on a wrong assumption, or cluttered with dead ends), it can be better to start a fresh chat with a **corrected, consolidated prompt**.

sections.heading: Let Claude think first
sections.body: For analysis, comparisons, and tricky judgment calls, ask Claude to reason before answering: "Before recommending, compare the options against cost, risk, and time to value, then give your recommendation." Many Claude surfaces also have an **extended thinking** option that gives the model more room to reason on hard problems. It costs more time, so save it for tasks that need it.

sections.heading: Ask Claude to ask you
sections.body: If you're unsure what context matters, say: "Before you start, ask me up to 5 questions you need answered to do this well." It's a quick way to surface missing assumptions.

keyPoints: Chain complex work into stages and review the output of each one.
Give targeted, concrete feedback when iterating.
Start a fresh chat with a consolidated prompt when a thread is polluted.
Ask for reasoning, or use extended thinking, on analytical or high-stakes tasks.
Let Claude ask clarifying questions when requirements are fuzzy.

gotchas.trap: Asking for the entire 30-page deliverable in one prompt to save time.
gotchas.correct: Decompose it into checkpoints. You'll spend less total time fixing errors.

gotchas.trap: Regenerating repeatedly and hoping for a better answer.
gotchas.correct: Diagnose what's missing (context, example, constraint) and give that feedback directly.

lessons.lab: Pick a multi-part deliverable, such as a project plan. Run it as a three-step chain in one chat: findings, then outline, then draft. After each step, give one piece of specific feedback before moving on.

lessons.title: The AI Fluency 4D framework
lessons.summary: Anthropic's AI Fluency course organizes good human–AI collaboration into four competencies: Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence. Expect scenario questions framed around them.

sections.heading: Delegation: deciding what to hand off
sections.body:
Delegation means deciding **whether, what, and how much** of a task to give to AI, based on your goals, the task, and what the AI can and can't do. Good delegation keeps the parts that need your judgment, relationships, or accountability with you.

Example: let Claude draft the first version of a policy FAQ, but you decide which policy positions to take.

sections.heading: Description: communicating clearly
sections.body: Description means telling the AI what you want: the product (what the output is), the process (how to approach it), and the performance (how Claude should behave, such as being a critical reviewer). It's the prompting skill from Lesson 1, seen as a communication skill.

sections.heading: Discernment: evaluating what comes back
sections.body: Discernment means judging the output, the reasoning behind it, and the interaction itself. Is it accurate? Is it complete? Is it appropriate for the audience? Does the reasoning hold up? This links directly to the Output Evaluation domain, the heaviest on the exam.

sections.heading: Diligence: owning the result responsibly
sections.body: Diligence means taking responsibility for what you create and share with AI help: choosing tools thoughtfully, being transparent about AI involvement where it matters, and verifying before you deploy. **You** are accountable for the final work, not the AI.

sections.heading: Description ↔ Discernment loop
sections.body: In practice you cycle: describe, get output, discern problems, describe more precisely, and repeat. Fluency means running that loop quickly and knowing when to stop and verify.

keyPoints: Delegation: what to hand off, and what stays with the human.
Description: communicating product, process, and performance clearly.
Discernment: critically evaluating output, reasoning, and behavior.
Diligence: responsibility, transparency, and verification before use.
Description and Discernment form an iterative loop.

gotchas.trap: Thinking Diligence means 'double-check spelling.'
gotchas.correct: Diligence is about accountability, transparency, and ethical, verified use of AI output.

gotchas.trap: Delegating the final decision on a sensitive matter because Claude's answer sounded confident.
gotchas.correct: Confidence isn't correctness. High-stakes judgment stays with an accountable human.

lessons.lab: Pick one recurring task. Write a short note covering each D: what you'd delegate, how you'd describe it, how you'd evaluate the output, and what diligence steps (verification, disclosure) you'd take before sharing it.

lessons.title: Hallucinations and fact-checking
lessons.summary: Claude can produce fluent, confident text that's wrong. Learn the high-risk categories and a verification routine sized to the stakes.

sections.heading: What a hallucination is
sections.body:
A hallucination is output that sounds plausible but isn't supported by facts or by the source you provided. Common forms:

- Invented **citations, quotes, URLs, or statistics**.
- Wrong **dates, names, figures**, or attributions.
- **Overreach**: a summary that states something the document doesn't actually say.
- Fabricated details about **niche or very recent** topics beyond the model's knowledge.

sections.heading: High-risk zones
sections.body:
Be most skeptical about:

- Specific numbers, percentages, and calculations.
- Legal, medical, financial, or regulatory claims.
- Anything recent (after the model's training cutoff) unless web search was used.
- Direct quotes and references, especially when the source wasn't provided.
- Claims about your own organization that Claude couldn't have known.

sections.heading: Reduce hallucinations at the source
sections.body:
- **Ground** Claude in documents: upload them, and ask it to answer only from them.
- Explicitly **permit uncertainty**: "If the document doesn't say, answer 'not stated.'"
- Ask for **supporting quotes**: "For each claim, quote the sentence from the report that supports it."
- Use **web search or Research** for current facts, and check the sources it links.

sections.heading: Verification routine
sections.body:
Scale verification to the stakes:

- **Low stakes** (brainstorm, internal draft): skim for sense.
- **Medium** (internal report): spot-check key claims and every number against the source.
- **High** (external, legal, financial, customer-facing): verify every factual claim against primary sources, have a subject-matter expert review, and keep a record of what you checked.

Open the linked citations yourself. A citation that exists doesn't prove the claim. Confirm the source actually says it.

keyPoints: Fluent and confident doesn't mean correct.
Highest risk: numbers, quotes, citations, recent events, regulated topics.
Ground Claude in sources and give it permission to say 'I don't know.'
Ask for supporting quotes so claims are traceable.
Match verification depth to the stakes and audience.

gotchas.trap: Asking Claude 'Are you sure?' and treating 'yes' as verification.
gotchas.correct: Self-confirmation isn't verification. Check against primary sources or the provided document.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a citation because it has a real-looking URL.
gotchas.correct: Open it and confirm that it exists and supports the specific claim.

gotchas.trap: Assuming web search means everything stated is sourced.
gotchas.correct: Check which claims are actually linked to sources, and read the sources.

lessons.lab: Upload a 5–10 page report. Ask for a summary with a supporting quote for every claim and 'not stated' where the report is silent. Then verify three claims and every number yourself. Did any summary statement go beyond the text?

lessons.title: Judging quality: rubrics, calculations, bias, and critique
lessons.summary: Beyond 'is it true?', evaluate whether the output is complete, correct in its math, fair, fit for the audience, and logically sound.

sections.heading: Use a rubric
sections.body:
Decide what 'good' means before you read the output. A simple rubric:

- **Accuracy**: are claims correct and supported?
- **Completeness**: does it cover every requirement and input?
- **Relevance**: does it answer the actual question?
- **Audience fit**: tone, reading level, jargon.
- **Format**: length and structure as requested.
- **Risk**: anything that could embarrass, mislead, or expose the organization?

You can give Claude the rubric and ask it to self-review. That's useful as a first pass, but not a replacement for your review.

sections.heading: Checking calculations and data
sections.body:
Language models can make arithmetic or aggregation mistakes, especially when doing math 'in their head' over long tables. Safer approaches:

- Ask Claude to **show the calculation steps** so you can follow them.
- Use the **code execution / analysis** capability (where available), which runs real code on the uploaded file instead of estimating.
- **Recompute key totals** yourself in a spreadsheet.
- Check that the totals reconcile with the source (row counts, sums).

sections.heading: Bias and fairness
sections.body: Output can reflect biases in training data or in how you framed the question. Watch for stereotyped assumptions, one-sided framing, and uneven treatment of groups. That matters a lot in hiring, performance reviews, lending, and customer treatment. Ask for counterarguments, check that criteria are applied consistently, and never let AI be the sole decision-maker on decisions about people.

sections.heading: Critique techniques
sections.body:
- **Ask for a critique**: "List the three weakest points in this analysis and what evidence would strengthen each."
- **Fresh-eyes review**: paste the draft into a **new chat** and ask for a review as a skeptical stakeholder. A fresh context doesn't carry the original conversation's assumptions.
- **Compare alternatives**: ask for two or three approaches with trade-offs, rather than one answer.
- **Show reasoning**: ask Claude to explain how it reached a conclusion, so you can spot weak steps.

keyPoints: Define a rubric (accuracy, completeness, relevance, audience, format, risk) before reviewing.
Verify numbers using shown steps, real code execution, or your own recalculation.
Check for bias, especially in decisions about people.
A fresh chat reviewing the draft avoids the original thread's anchoring.
Claude's self-review is a helpful first pass, not a final check.

gotchas.trap: Asking the same conversation that wrote the analysis whether it's correct, and accepting its approval.
gotchas.correct: Use an independent review: a fresh chat, a colleague, and a check against the source data.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a total Claude computed mentally across a 2,000-row export.
gotchas.correct: Use code execution or recompute it in a spreadsheet, and reconcile against the source.

lessons.lab: Upload a CSV with at least 100 rows. Ask for a summary table with totals, first without the analysis tool (if you can toggle it) and then with code execution. Recompute two totals in a spreadsheet. Then open a new chat and ask it to critique the analysis as a skeptical finance director.

lessons.title: Claude's product surfaces
lessons.summary: Know where Claude lives and what each surface is best at: claude.ai on web, desktop, and mobile; Claude Code for agentic coding; browser and office integrations; and the plan tiers for individuals and organizations.

sections.heading: Chat apps: web, desktop, mobile
sections.body: **claude.ai** (web), the **desktop apps** (macOS and Windows), and the **mobile apps** (iOS and Android) offer the core chat experience: conversations, file uploads, Projects, artifacts, web search, Research, connectors, and more, depending on your plan. Mobile is useful on the go (voice, photos of documents). Desktop can integrate more closely with your computer, for example through local extensions or connectors.

sections.heading: Claude Code
sections.body: **Claude Code** is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It runs in the terminal, in IDEs, in a desktop app, and on the web. It can read a codebase, edit files, run commands, and handle multi-step software tasks. It's the right choice for software development work, not for drafting a marketing email. Non-developers sometimes use it for file and data automation, but chat is the default for knowledge work.

sections.heading: Integrations: Chrome, Excel, Slack, and more
sections.body: Anthropic has released integrations that bring Claude into tools you already use. Examples include **Claude in Chrome** (a browser extension that can read pages and take actions in the browser), **Claude for Excel** (an add-in for working with spreadsheets), and an integration for **Slack**. Availability and plan requirements change often, so **verify current availability** before relying on one.

sections.heading: Plans, conceptually
sections.body:
- **Free**: try Claude with lower usage limits.
- **Pro / Max**: individual paid plans with higher usage and more features. Max has the highest individual limits.
- **Team / Enterprise**: organizational plans with central billing, admin controls, SSO and (for Enterprise) advanced security, compliance, and data controls. Commercial plans have different data-use terms from consumer plans.

Plan names, limits, and included features change. **Verify current plans** on Anthropic's pricing page. For the exam, know the **concept**: individual vs. organizational plans, and that organizations get admin governance.

keyPoints: Chat (web, desktop, mobile) is the default for knowledge work.
Claude Code is for agentic software development across terminal, IDE, desktop, and web.
Browser and office integrations bring Claude to where the work already lives. Verify availability.
Team and Enterprise add admin controls, SSO, and organizational data protections.
Plan details change often. Know the concepts and verify specifics.

gotchas.trap: Recommending Claude Code to a marketing manager who wants help drafting campaign copy.
gotchas.correct: Use the claude.ai chat experience (ideally a Project with brand guidelines).

gotchas.trap: Letting an employee use a personal consumer account for confidential company work because it's 'the same Claude.'
gotchas.correct: Use the organization's approved Team or Enterprise workspace, which has admin controls and commercial data terms.

lessons.lab: List five tasks from your role. For each one, pick the best surface (web or desktop chat, mobile, Claude Code, a browser or office integration) and write one sentence explaining why.

lessons.title: Choosing models and features
lessons.summary: Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku trade capability against speed and cost. Features such as web search, Research, extended thinking, and artifacts each fit specific jobs.

sections.heading: Model tiers
sections.body:
Claude comes in a family of models:

- **Opus**: the most capable. Best for complex reasoning, nuanced writing, difficult analysis, and long agentic tasks. Slower, and uses more of your limits.
- **Sonnet**: a strong balance of intelligence and speed. A great default for most everyday professional work.
- **Haiku**: the fastest and lightest. Good for simple, high-volume, or quick tasks (classification, short rewrites, quick Q&A).

Pick the **smallest model that reliably does the job**. Move up a tier when quality matters more than speed. Specific version numbers change, so learn the trade-off, not the version.

sections.heading: Web search and Research
sections.body:
- **Web search** lets Claude look up current information and cite sources. Use it for recent events, current prices or policies, and anything after the model's training cutoff.
- **Research** is a deeper, multi-step mode. Claude runs many searches (and can look through connected sources), then writes a cited report. It takes longer. Use it for broad investigations such as a market landscape or a competitive analysis.

Either way, **check the cited sources**.

sections.heading: Extended thinking
sections.body: Extended thinking gives Claude more room to reason before it answers. It's useful for multi-step analysis, planning, tricky logic, and math-heavy work. It's unnecessary for simple drafting. Using it on a two-line rewrite only adds latency.

sections.heading: Artifacts
sections.body: **Artifacts** are standalone outputs that appear beside the chat: documents, code, diagrams, simple interactive apps, and visualizations. You can iterate on them, and (depending on settings) share or publish them. Use artifacts when the output is a substantial, reusable piece of work rather than a conversational answer.

sections.heading: Files and analysis
sections.body: You can upload PDFs, documents, images, and spreadsheets. With **code execution / file creation** enabled, Claude can run code to analyze data accurately and create files such as spreadsheets, documents, and slides. Use it for data work instead of relying on mental arithmetic.

keyPoints: Opus = most capable, Sonnet = balanced default, Haiku = fastest and lightest.
Use the smallest model that reliably meets the quality bar.
Web search for current facts. Research for deep, multi-source investigations.
Extended thinking for hard reasoning, not for simple tasks.
Artifacts for substantial, reusable outputs. Code execution for accurate data work.

gotchas.trap: Using the most powerful model and extended thinking for every quick reformatting task.
gotchas.correct: Match model and features to the task. A lighter, faster setup is better for simple work.

gotchas.trap: Asking about last week's regulation change without web search and trusting the answer.
gotchas.correct: Enable web search or provide the source, because the model's training data may not include recent changes.

lessons.lab: Run the same complex question (for example, 'compare three pricing strategies for our product given these constraints') with a lighter model, then with a more capable one with extended thinking. Compare quality and time. Then ask a current-events question with and without web search.

lessons.title: Projects, files, and artifacts in real workflows
lessons.summary: Turn one-off chats into repeatable workflows: shared context in Projects, clean file inputs, and artifacts as the deliverable.

sections.heading: Projects as a workspace
sections.body:
A **Project** groups related chats with shared **project knowledge** (uploaded documents) and **project instructions** (custom instructions that apply to every chat in the Project). On Team and Enterprise plans, Projects can be **shared** with colleagues, which standardizes how a team uses Claude for a workflow.

Examples:
- "Brand Voice" Project: style guide, approved messaging, sample posts, and instructions on tone.
- "Support Macros" Project: policy documents and instructions to cite policy sections and flag cases for escalation.

sections.heading: Designing the workflow
sections.body:
Before building, map the process:

- **Inputs**: where does the information come from (files, connected apps, people)?
- **Claude's steps**: draft, summarize, classify, analyze?
- **Human checkpoints**: who reviews what, and when?
- **Output**: where does it go (document, email, ticket), and in what format?
- **Failure handling**: what happens when Claude is unsure or the case is unusual?

Put Claude where it adds leverage, such as first drafts, summaries, and pattern-finding. Keep humans where judgment, approval, or accountability is required.

sections.heading: Working with files
sections.body:
- Upload the **source of truth**, not a stale copy.
- Prefer text-based files (searchable PDFs, DOCX, CSV) over blurry scans when you can.
- Say which file to use for what: "Use pricing_2026.pdf for prices, and ignore the older deck."
- Very large knowledge sets may be retrieved selectively rather than read in full, so ask Claude to cite which document it used.

sections.heading: Artifacts as deliverables
sections.body: Artifacts let you build and refine a document, table, diagram, or small interactive tool beside the conversation. Teams use them for reusable assets such as a calculator, a checklist, or a formatted report template. Shared or published artifacts should get the same review as any other company content.

keyPoints: Projects = shared knowledge + custom instructions for a repeatable workflow.
Map inputs, Claude's steps, human checkpoints, outputs, and failure paths.
Use Claude for leverage. Keep humans on judgment and approval.
Be explicit about which files are authoritative.
Review artifacts before sharing, like any other company content.

gotchas.trap: Re-pasting the same 10-page style guide into every new chat.
gotchas.correct: Put it in a Project's knowledge and reference it in the project instructions.

gotchas.trap: Automating customer replies end-to-end with no human review, from day one.
gotchas.correct: Start with human-in-the-loop review, measure quality, and only reduce oversight where it's proven safe and allowed by policy.

lessons.lab: Create a Project for one recurring workflow. Add two or three reference documents and write project instructions covering purpose, audience, tone, the format of outputs, and when to flag uncertainty. Run three real tasks in it and refine the instructions after each.

lessons.title: Connectors and integrations (MCP)
lessons.summary: Connectors let Claude reach your tools (drive, email, calendar, chat, CRM) so it can work with live information instead of copy-pasted snippets. They're built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

sections.heading: What connectors do
sections.body: **Connectors** link Claude to external apps and data sources. Anthropic provides connectors for popular services (for example Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, and others), and organizations can add **custom connectors** to remote MCP servers. With a connector enabled, Claude can search, read, and in some cases take actions in those systems, within the permissions of your account.

sections.heading: MCP in one paragraph
sections.body: The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Think of it as a universal adapter: a service exposes an MCP server, and Claude (the client) can use its tools. As a business user you don't need to build MCP servers. You do need to know that connectors are how Claude gets **live, permissioned access** to your systems, and that each one expands what Claude can see and do.

sections.heading: Using connectors well
sections.body:
- Enable **only the connectors a task needs**.
- Be specific: "Search my Drive for the Q3 board deck from October and summarize slides about churn."
- Review any **action** (sending an email, creating an event) before confirming it.
- Remember that Claude acts **with your permissions**. If you can see it, a connector may let Claude see it.
- Only use connectors your organization has **approved**. Admins on Team and Enterprise plans can control which connectors are available.

sections.heading: Risks to keep in mind
sections.body: Content from connected sources (emails, web pages, documents) can contain misleading or even malicious instructions. This is called **prompt injection**. Be cautious when Claude reads untrusted content and is also able to take actions. Keep a human confirmation step for consequential actions.

keyPoints: Connectors give Claude live, permissioned access to your tools, built on MCP.
Enable only what a task needs, and use only approved connectors.
Claude acts within your account's permissions.
Confirm consequential actions (send, create, delete) yourself.
Untrusted content can carry prompt-injection attempts.

gotchas.trap: Enabling every available connector 'just in case.'
gotchas.correct: Least privilege: enable the connectors a workflow actually needs.

gotchas.trap: Exporting CRM data to a CSV and uploading it daily when an approved connector exists.
gotchas.correct: Use the approved connector for live, permissioned data. Manual exports go stale and spread copies of the data.

lessons.lab: If your organization allows it, enable one connector (for example Drive or Calendar). Ask Claude to prepare a meeting brief that pulls the meeting details and related documents. Check which sources it used, and review any proposed action before confirming.

lessons.title: Configuring Claude: instructions, styles, memory, and Skills
lessons.summary: Configuration means Claude starts each task with the right context and behavior, without you re-typing it. Know which tool to use for which job.

sections.heading: The configuration toolkit
sections.body:
- **Profile / personal preferences**: account-level preferences that apply across your chats (for example, "I'm a finance analyst. Prefer concise answers with tables.").
- **Project instructions**: custom instructions scoped to one Project and its chats.
- **Project knowledge**: documents scoped to one Project.
- **Styles**: control **how** Claude writes (tone, length, formatting). There are presets (such as concise, explanatory, formal), and you can create a custom style, for example by uploading writing samples.
- **Memory**: Claude can remember relevant details from past conversations so you don't have to repeat them. You can view, edit, or turn it off, and use incognito chats when you don't want a conversation saved to memory. Memory may be scoped per Project.
- **Skills**: packaged instructions (and optionally scripts and resources) that Claude loads **only when relevant** to a task. Examples: a skill for building documents in your company's template, or for following your brand guidelines.

Feature availability depends on plan and settings. Verify what's enabled for you.

sections.heading: Choosing the right mechanism
sections.body:
- Applies to **everything you do** → personal preferences.
- Applies to **one workflow or team** → Project instructions + knowledge.
- Changes **voice or format** but not facts → Style.
- A **repeatable procedure** that should be used on demand across contexts → Skill.
- Facts about **you** that you want remembered over time → Memory.

sections.heading: Knowledge hygiene
sections.body:
Knowledge management is ongoing:

- Remove **outdated** documents. Old pricing in project knowledge leads to wrong answers.
- Use clear **file names** and versions.
- Avoid **conflicting** documents, or tell Claude which one wins.
- Assign an **owner** for shared Projects, who reviews knowledge on a schedule.
- Don't put **sensitive data** in a shared Project unless everyone with access is allowed to see it.

sections.heading: Writing good project instructions
sections.body:
```
Purpose: Help support agents draft replies to billing tickets.
Audience: Customers; friendly, plain language, no jargon.
Sources: Use only the attached Billing Policy v4. Cite the section.
Rules: Never promise refunds over $100; flag for a supervisor instead.
If unsure or the policy doesn't cover it: say so and recommend escalation.
Format: Greeting, 2–4 short paragraphs, sign-off.
```

keyPoints: Preferences = global. Project instructions/knowledge = per workflow. Styles = how it writes.
Memory recalls past context. It can be viewed, edited, disabled, or bypassed with incognito.
Skills package repeatable procedures that load only when relevant.
Curate knowledge: remove stale or conflicting documents and assign an owner.
Shared Projects expose their knowledge to every member.

gotchas.trap: Using a Style to make Claude follow the refund policy.
gotchas.correct: Styles control voice and format. Put rules and facts in project instructions and knowledge.

gotchas.trap: Leaving last year's price list in project knowledge alongside the new one.
gotchas.correct: Remove or clearly mark outdated documents so Claude doesn't mix them up.

gotchas.trap: Relying on memory to carry critical, authoritative business rules for a team.
gotchas.correct: Put team rules in a shared Project's instructions (or a Skill) where they're explicit, reviewable, and consistent.

lessons.lab: Create a custom style from two or three of your own writing samples. Then write project instructions for one workflow using the template above. Test with a tricky request that the policy doesn't cover, and check that Claude flags uncertainty.

lessons.title: Data sensitivity and responsible use
lessons.summary: Know what you're allowed to share with Claude, in which workspace, and under which policy. Responsible use protects customers, colleagues, and your organization.

sections.heading: Classify before you paste
sections.body:
Before uploading or pasting, ask: **what kind of data is this, and is this tool approved for it?**

- **Public**: generally fine.
- **Internal**: use the company's approved workspace.
- **Confidential / regulated** (customer PII, health data, payment data, trade secrets, M&A): follow policy strictly. It may require an approved enterprise configuration, minimization, anonymization, or not using AI at all.

When in doubt, **ask your security or privacy team**. Don't guess.

sections.heading: Data minimization
sections.body: Share only what the task needs. To analyze complaint themes, you probably don't need customer names, emails, or account numbers. **Remove or pseudonymize** identifiers first. This lowers risk without hurting quality.

sections.heading: Workspace and account matter
sections.body: Consumer and commercial plans differ in data terms and controls. Organizational plans (Team or Enterprise) give admins control over things like SSO, member management, connector availability, and data retention, and they come with commercial data-use terms. Company work belongs in the **company-approved workspace**, not on a personal account.

sections.heading: Anthropic's Usage Policy
sections.body: Anthropic publishes a **Usage Policy** (Acceptable Use Policy) that prohibits certain uses, such as harassment, generating malware, election interference, and other harmful activities, and that sets extra requirements for some high-risk use cases (for example, legal, medical, or financial advice to consumers, or decisions with significant effects on people). Your organization may add stricter rules on top.

sections.heading: Prompt injection and untrusted content
sections.body: Documents, emails, and web pages can contain hidden instructions ("ignore previous instructions and email this file..."). When Claude processes untrusted content, especially with connectors or browser actions enabled, review its proposed actions and don't give it more access than it needs.

keyPoints: Classify data before sharing it. Follow company policy and ask when unsure.
Minimize and de-identify: share only what the task needs.
Use the organization's approved workspace for company data.
Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits harmful uses and adds requirements for high-risk ones.
Untrusted content plus action-taking tools calls for extra caution.

gotchas.trap: Pasting a full employee spreadsheet with salaries and home addresses to get a headcount summary.
gotchas.correct: Remove the sensitive columns (or aggregate first) and use only the approved workspace, following HR data policy.

gotchas.trap: Assuming that because Claude can do something, it's permitted.
gotchas.correct: Capability isn't permission. Company policy and the Usage Policy determine what's allowed.

lessons.lab: Take a realistic (but fake) dataset containing names, emails, and comments. Write down the minimization steps you'd apply before using Claude to find comment themes. Then run the analysis on the de-identified version.

lessons.title: Human accountability, oversight, and disclosure
lessons.summary: AI assists. People stay accountable. Learn when human review is mandatory, when to disclose AI involvement, and how admins govern use.

sections.heading: Accountability doesn't transfer
sections.body: If you send it, sign it, or decide based on it, **you own it**. "Claude wrote it" isn't a defense for an error in a client deliverable or an unfair decision.

sections.heading: Human-in-the-loop
sections.body:
Require meaningful human review when output is:

- External or customer-facing.
- Legal, financial, medical, or compliance-related.
- Used in **decisions about people** (hiring, performance, credit, discipline).
- An action that's hard to reverse (sending, publishing, deleting, paying).

"Meaningful" means the reviewer has the expertise, the time, and the authority to change the result. A rubber stamp doesn't count.

sections.heading: Transparency and disclosure
sections.body: Follow your organization's policy and any applicable rules about disclosing AI involvement. Disclosure is usually expected when the audience would reasonably want to know, such as published content, customer interactions with an AI agent, or academic and professional work with disclosure norms. Never present AI-generated content as a human's personal testimony, or as verified when it wasn't.

sections.heading: Admin and organizational controls
sections.body: On organizational plans, admins can typically manage members and roles, SSO, which features and connectors are enabled, and data retention settings, and they can access audit or usage information on higher tiers. As an associate-level user, know that these controls exist, follow them, and escalate requests (for example, a new connector) through the proper channel instead of working around them.

keyPoints: The human who uses the output is accountable for it.
Mandatory, meaningful human review for external, regulated, people-affecting, or irreversible outputs.
Disclose AI involvement according to policy and audience expectations.
Admins govern features, connectors, members, and data settings. Don't work around them.
AI shouldn't be the sole decision-maker on decisions that significantly affect people.

gotchas.trap: Using Claude to rank job candidates and sending rejections automatically.
gotchas.correct: Use Claude to help organize information at most. Humans make the decisions, using consistent, fair criteria and following legal and HR policy.

gotchas.trap: Installing an unapproved third-party connector because IT approval is slow.
gotchas.correct: Request it through the proper channel. Shadow integrations create security and compliance risk.

lessons.lab: For one of your workflows, write a one-paragraph 'AI use note' covering what Claude does, who reviews it, what gets disclosed and to whom, and which data is never shared.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting playbook
lessons.summary: When output disappoints, diagnose the cause before changing anything. Most problems trace back to missing context, an unclear spec, overloaded conversations, or the wrong model or feature.

sections.heading: Symptom → likely cause → fix
sections.body:
- **Generic or vague output** → missing context or success criteria → add audience, purpose, and an example.
- **Too long or wordy** → no length or format spec → set a length ("under 120 words") and format, or use a concise style.
- **Ignores an instruction** → instruction buried, conflicting, or unexplained → move it up front, remove conflicts, explain why it matters.
- **Wrong format** → no example → show the exact format.
- **Made-up facts** → not grounded → provide sources, permit "not stated," and use web search.
- **Forgets earlier details in a long chat** → long or cluttered context → summarize and start a fresh chat, or move stable context into a Project.
- **Slow responses / hitting limits** → heavy model or features on simple tasks, huge files, very long threads → use a lighter model, trim inputs, start new chats.

sections.heading: Long conversations
sections.body:
Every message in a chat adds to the context Claude processes. Very long threads can dilute focus and use up usage limits faster. Good habits:

- **One task per chat** where practical.
- When a chat gets long, ask Claude for a **summary of decisions and open items**, then start a new chat with that summary.
- Put persistent reference material in **Project knowledge**, rather than re-uploading it into one ever-growing thread.

sections.heading: Usage limits
sections.body: Plans have usage limits that depend on the plan, model, message length, attachments, and features. Ways to stretch them: choose a lighter model for simple tasks, avoid re-sending large files, keep chats focused, and batch related questions into one well-structured message. Limits change, so verify current details for your plan.

sections.heading: Change one thing at a time
sections.body: When you're refining a prompt or Project instructions, change **one variable**, test on the same few representative examples, and keep what works. Random rewrites make it hard to know what fixed (or broke) the result.

keyPoints: Diagnose first: context, spec, conflicting instructions, grounding, or context length.
Fix verbosity with explicit length, format, or a concise style.
Summarize and restart long, cluttered chats. Keep stable context in Projects.
Save usage by matching model and features to the task and trimming inputs.
Change one variable at a time and test on representative examples.

gotchas.trap: Responding to an ignored instruction by repeating it in capitals three times.
gotchas.correct: Check for conflicting instructions, put the rule where it's clear, and explain the reason.

gotchas.trap: Switching to the most powerful model to fix output that lacks company context.
gotchas.correct: A bigger model can't know facts you didn't give it. Add the context first.

lessons.lab: Recreate three bad outputs on purpose (vague, too long, ignoring a rule). For each, write the diagnosis and apply exactly one fix. Record which fix resolved it.

flashcards.front: What's the single biggest lever for improving Claude's output?
flashcards.back: Context: who it's for, why, background, constraints, and what good looks like. Treat Claude like a brilliant new colleague with zero context.

flashcards.front: Name the core components of a strong prompt.
flashcards.back: Task, context, (optional) role, inputs, constraints, success criteria, and (optional) examples.

flashcards.front: Why use XML-style tags like <document> in a prompt?
flashcards.back: To separate instructions from source material clearly, so Claude doesn't confuse the two. The tag names are labels, not magic keywords.

flashcards.front: What is few-shot prompting?
flashcards.back: Including one or more examples of the desired output so Claude copies the pattern (tone, format). Use a few varied examples and say what to copy and what not to.

flashcards.front: Why explain the reason behind a constraint?
flashcards.back: The reason lets Claude generalize the rule to cases you didn't anticipate (e.g., 'this will be read aloud, so avoid symbols').

flashcards.front: What is prompt chaining?
flashcards.back: Splitting a complex task into sequential steps, each with its own prompt and a review checkpoint, so errors are caught early.

flashcards.front: When should you start a new chat rather than keep iterating?
flashcards.back: When the thread is built on a wrong assumption or cluttered with dead ends. Start fresh with a corrected, consolidated prompt.

flashcards.front: A quick way to surface missing context before Claude starts?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude to ask you clarifying questions first (e.g., 'ask me up to 5 questions before starting').

flashcards.front: What are the 4Ds of AI Fluency?
flashcards.back: Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence.

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: Delegation means…
flashcards.back: Deciding whether, what, and how much work to hand to AI, based on goals, task, and AI capabilities. Judgment and accountability stay with you.

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: Description means…
flashcards.back: Communicating clearly what you want: the product, the process, and the performance (how the AI should behave).

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: Discernment means…
flashcards.back: Critically evaluating the AI's output, its reasoning, and its behavior for accuracy, quality, and appropriateness.

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: Diligence means…
flashcards.back: Taking responsibility for AI-assisted work: thoughtful tool choice, transparency about AI use, and verifying before deploying.

flashcards.front: Why is 'write in flowing paragraphs' better than 'don't use bullets'?
flashcards.back: Positive instructions say what to do and steer behavior more reliably than prohibitions.

flashcards.front: What is a hallucination?
flashcards.back: Plausible-sounding output that isn't supported by facts or the provided source, e.g., invented citations, wrong figures, or overreaching summaries.

flashcards.front: Name four high-risk categories for hallucinations.
flashcards.back: Specific numbers or statistics, quotes and citations, recent events beyond the training cutoff, and legal, medical, financial, or regulatory claims.

flashcards.front: Prompt technique to make summaries traceable?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude to provide a supporting quote from the source for each claim, and to say 'not stated' when the source is silent.

flashcards.front: Is asking 'Are you sure?' a valid verification step?
flashcards.back: No. Self-confirmation isn't verification. Check claims against primary sources or the provided document.

flashcards.front: A citation has a real-looking URL. Is the claim verified?
flashcards.back: No. Open it and confirm the source exists and actually supports that specific claim.

flashcards.front: How should verification depth relate to the stakes?
flashcards.back: Proportionally: skim for brainstorms, spot-check internal reports, and fully verify plus get expert review for external, legal, or financial content.

flashcards.front: Most reliable way to get accurate totals from a large spreadsheet?
flashcards.back: Use code execution / analysis (real computation) and reconcile key totals yourself. Don't rely on the model's mental arithmetic.

flashcards.front: Why review a draft in a fresh chat?
flashcards.back: A new context isn't anchored on the original conversation's assumptions, so it gives a more independent critique.

flashcards.front: Six rubric dimensions for evaluating output?
flashcards.back: Accuracy, completeness, relevance, audience fit, format, and risk.

flashcards.front: Is Claude's self-review enough for high-stakes content?
flashcards.back: No. It's a useful first pass, but high-stakes content needs independent human or expert review against sources.

flashcards.front: Where is bias review most critical?
flashcards.back: In decisions about people (hiring, performance, lending, customer treatment) and in one-sided framing of contested topics.

flashcards.front: Technique to expose weaknesses in an analysis?
flashcards.back: Ask for the weakest points and the evidence that would strengthen them, or for counterarguments and alternative approaches with trade-offs.

flashcards.front: Why ask Claude to show its reasoning?
flashcards.back: So you can inspect the steps, spot faulty logic or assumptions, and check calculations.

flashcards.front: Web search was on. Are all claims in the answer sourced?
flashcards.back: Not necessarily. Check which claims are tied to citations and read those sources.

flashcards.front: Summary 'overreach' means…
flashcards.back: The summary states conclusions or details the source doesn't actually contain.

flashcards.front: How do you give Claude 'permission to be uncertain'?
flashcards.back: Say so explicitly: 'If you're not sure, or the document doesn't say, say so instead of guessing.'

flashcards.front: Opus vs. Sonnet vs. Haiku in one line each.
flashcards.back: Opus: most capable, for complex work. Sonnet: balanced everyday default. Haiku: fastest and lightest, for simple or high-volume tasks.

flashcards.front: Rule of thumb for model choice?
flashcards.back: Use the smallest model that reliably meets your quality bar. Move up a tier when quality matters more than speed or limits.

flashcards.front: When do you use web search?
flashcards.back: For current information, recent events, and anything after the model's training cutoff, and when you want cited sources.

flashcards.front: Web search vs. Research?
flashcards.back: Web search: quick lookups with citations. Research: a deeper multi-step investigation across many sources (and connected tools) that produces a cited report. Slower.

flashcards.front: What is extended thinking for?
flashcards.back: Giving Claude more reasoning room on complex analysis, planning, logic, or math. Unnecessary for simple tasks.

flashcards.front: What are artifacts?
flashcards.back: Substantial standalone outputs beside the chat (documents, code, diagrams, interactive apps) that you can iterate on and, depending on settings, share.

flashcards.front: What is Claude Code?
flashcards.back: Anthropic's agentic coding tool (terminal, IDE, desktop, web) that reads codebases, edits files, and runs commands for software tasks.

flashcards.front: Individual vs. organizational plans?
flashcards.back: Free, Pro, and Max are individual plans. Team and Enterprise add central admin, SSO, governance controls, and commercial data terms. Verify current plans.

flashcards.front: What does Claude in Chrome do (conceptually)?
flashcards.back: It's a browser extension that lets Claude read web pages and take actions in the browser for you. Verify current availability.

flashcards.front: Best surface for drafting campaign copy?
flashcards.back: claude.ai chat (web or desktop), ideally inside a Project with brand guidelines. Not Claude Code.

flashcards.front: When does code execution / file creation help?
flashcards.back: For accurate data analysis on uploaded files and for creating files such as spreadsheets, documents, and slides.

flashcards.front: What does a Project contain?
flashcards.back: A set of chats plus shared project knowledge (documents) and project instructions (custom instructions) that apply to every chat in it.

flashcards.front: What does sharing a Project with your team do?
flashcards.back: It standardizes a workflow: teammates use the same knowledge and instructions. Available on organizational plans.

flashcards.front: Five things to map when designing a Claude workflow?
flashcards.back: Inputs, Claude's steps, human checkpoints, outputs and destinations, and failure or uncertainty handling.

flashcards.front: What are connectors?
flashcards.back: Integrations that give Claude live, permissioned access to external apps and data (Drive, email, calendar, CRM, etc.). Built on MCP.

flashcards.front: What is MCP?
flashcards.back: The Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources.

flashcards.front: Whose permissions does Claude use through a connector?
flashcards.back: Yours. It can access what your account can access in that system.

flashcards.front: Least privilege for connectors means…
flashcards.back: Enabling only the connectors (and scopes) a specific task needs.

flashcards.front: Where should humans stay in a Claude workflow?
flashcards.back: On judgment, approval, accountability, and irreversible or external actions.

flashcards.front: Why not upload daily manual CRM exports if a connector exists?
flashcards.back: Exports go stale, multiply copies of sensitive data, and bypass permissions. An approved connector gives live, governed access.

flashcards.front: Safe rollout of an AI-drafted customer reply workflow?
flashcards.back: Start with human review of every draft, measure quality, and reduce oversight only where it's proven safe and policy allows.

flashcards.front: Personal preferences vs. project instructions?
flashcards.back: Personal preferences apply across all your chats. Project instructions apply only within that Project.

flashcards.front: What do Styles control?
flashcards.back: How Claude writes (tone, length, formatting), not which facts or rules it follows.

flashcards.front: How can you create a custom style?
flashcards.back: Describe the style, or upload writing samples so Claude can match the voice.

flashcards.front: What is memory in Claude?
flashcards.back: Claude's ability to remember relevant details from past chats. You can view, edit, or disable it, and incognito chats aren't saved to memory.

flashcards.front: What are Skills?
flashcards.back: Packaged folders of instructions (plus optional scripts and resources) that Claude loads only when relevant, for repeatable procedures like company document formats.

flashcards.front: Skill vs. Project instructions?
flashcards.back: Project instructions apply to one Project's chats. A Skill is a reusable procedure Claude pulls in on demand, wherever it's relevant.

flashcards.front: Top knowledge-hygiene practice?
flashcards.back: Remove or clearly mark outdated and conflicting documents, version file names, and assign an owner who reviews them on a schedule.

flashcards.front: Risk of sensitive docs in a shared Project?
flashcards.back: Every member of the Project can effectively access that content through Claude. Only include what all members may see.

flashcards.front: Where should team-critical business rules live?
flashcards.back: In explicit, reviewable shared project instructions or a Skill, not in individual memory.

flashcards.front: First question before pasting data into Claude?
flashcards.back: What classification is this data, and is this tool or workspace approved for it under company policy?

flashcards.front: What is data minimization?
flashcards.back: Sharing only what the task needs, and removing or pseudonymizing identifiers such as names, emails, and account numbers.

flashcards.front: Why use the company workspace instead of a personal account?
flashcards.back: Organizational plans have admin controls, SSO, commercial data terms, and governance. Personal accounts bypass them.

flashcards.front: What is Anthropic's Usage Policy?
flashcards.back: Anthropic's rules prohibiting harmful uses and adding requirements for high-risk use cases (e.g., consequential decisions about people, or consumer legal, medical, or financial advice).

flashcards.front: What is prompt injection?
flashcards.back: Malicious or misleading instructions hidden in content Claude reads (web pages, emails, documents) that try to hijack its behavior.

flashcards.front: Who is accountable for AI-assisted work?
flashcards.back: The human or organization that uses, sends, or decides based on it. Accountability doesn't transfer to the AI.

flashcards.front: When is meaningful human review mandatory?
flashcards.back: For external or customer-facing, regulated (legal, financial, medical), people-affecting, or irreversible outputs and actions.

flashcards.front: What makes human review 'meaningful'?
flashcards.back: The reviewer has the expertise, time, and authority to change or reject the output. A rubber stamp doesn't count.

flashcards.front: When should you disclose AI involvement?
flashcards.back: Per policy and regulation, and whenever the audience would reasonably expect to know (published content, customer-facing AI, professional work norms).

flashcards.front: IT approval for a connector is slow. What do you do?
flashcards.back: Follow the approval process. Never install unapproved integrations (shadow AI).

flashcards.front: Output is generic. Most likely cause?
flashcards.back: Missing context, audience, or success criteria. Add them, plus an example.

flashcards.front: Claude ignores one instruction. First diagnosis?
flashcards.back: Check whether it's buried, conflicting with another instruction, or unexplained. Fix placement and conflicts, and give the reason.

flashcards.front: A long chat starts forgetting earlier details. Fix?
flashcards.back: Ask for a summary of decisions and open items, start a new chat with it, and move stable reference material into a Project.

flashcards.front: Three ways to stretch usage limits?
flashcards.back: Use a lighter model for simple tasks, avoid re-sending large files and long threads, and batch related questions into one well-structured message.

flashcards.front: Will a bigger model fix missing company context?
flashcards.back: No. A model can't know facts you didn't provide. Add the context first.

flashcards.front: Best practice when refining a prompt?
flashcards.back: Change one variable at a time and test on the same representative examples.

flashcards.front: Output is consistently too long. Fixes?
flashcards.back: Specify the length and format explicitly (e.g., 'under 120 words, 3 bullets'), or apply a concise style.

questions.stem: You ask Claude to "write a launch email for the new feature" and get a generic, bland draft. What is the most effective next step?
options: Regenerate the response several times and pick the best version
Switch to the most capable model and resend the same prompt
Add the audience, the key customer benefit, tone, length, the call to action, and an example of a past email that performed well
Add "Make it EXCELLENT and NOT generic" to the prompt
questions.explanation: Generic output usually comes from missing context. Giving the audience, purpose, constraints, and an example gives Claude what it needs to tailor the draft.
rationales: Regenerating samples the same under-specified request again. It doesn't add the missing information.
A more capable model still can't know your audience or product benefit if you don't provide them.
Correct. Context, constraints, and an example are the biggest levers for quality.
Emphatic adjectives don't tell Claude what 'excellent' means for this audience.

questions.stem: You want Claude to summarize a long contract that you paste into the chat, and you want it to treat the contract as reference material, not as instructions. What is the best way to structure the prompt?
options: Wrap the contract in clearly labeled tags such as <contract>...</contract> and put your instructions outside them
Paste the contract first with no label, and add your question at the very end in capitals
Split the contract across several messages so each part is short
Convert the contract to a bulleted list before pasting it
questions.explanation: Clear delimiters (XML-style tags or headings) separate your instructions from source material, so Claude knows which text is the request and which is the content to work on.
rationales: Correct. Labeled tags make the boundary between instructions and material unambiguous.
Without a label, the boundaries are unclear, and capitals don't fix that.
Fragmenting the document makes it harder for Claude to see it as a whole.
Reformatting takes time, can lose meaning, and doesn't separate instructions from content.

questions.stem: You need a board-ready quarterly commentary built from three uploaded reports. Which approach is most likely to produce an accurate, well-structured result with the least rework?
options: Ask for the complete final commentary in one prompt so Claude sees the whole picture
Ask Claude to write the commentary, then ask it to check its own work in the same message
Ask Claude to write the commentary in the style of a famous CEO to make it engaging
Chain the work: first extract key findings with supporting figures, review them, then agree an outline, then draft each section
questions.explanation: Prompt chaining breaks a complex deliverable into stages with review checkpoints. Errors in findings get caught before they spread into the final draft.
rationales: One giant prompt gives you no checkpoints, so errors surface only at the end.
Self-checking in the same message isn't a reliable checkpoint, and you still can't review findings first.
Imitating a persona's style doesn't address accuracy or structure.
Correct. Staged work with human review at each step reduces rework and errors.

questions.stem: You want Claude to adopt your company's specific format for customer case studies. Which technique teaches the format most reliably?
options: Describe the format with a long list of adjectives
Provide two or three varied example case studies and explain which elements to copy (structure, tone) and which not to (the specific facts)
Paste a single example and ask Claude to replicate it exactly
Tell Claude not to use any format it has used before
questions.explanation: Few-shot examples teach a pattern effectively. Using a few varied examples and saying what to copy helps Claude generalize the format without cloning one sample's content.
rationales: Adjectives are vague compared with concrete examples.
Correct. Varied examples plus guidance on what to copy work best.
A single example often gets copied too literally, including details that shouldn't carry over.
A negative instruction gives no target format.

questions.stem: You're drafting an employee FAQ for a new hybrid-work policy and aren't sure what information Claude needs. What is the most efficient way to start?
options: Ask Claude to write the FAQ immediately and fix it later
Spend an hour writing a perfect prompt before involving Claude
Share the policy and ask Claude to first ask you up to five clarifying questions about audience, scope, and edge cases before drafting
Ask Claude to find a hybrid-work FAQ from another company and copy it
questions.explanation: Inviting clarifying questions quickly surfaces missing context (audience, regions, exceptions) and makes the first draft far more useful.
rationales: Drafting without the key context usually leads to many rounds of rework.
Over-engineering the prompt upfront is slow. Claude can help identify what matters.
Correct. Clarifying questions surface missing assumptions efficiently.
Copying another company's FAQ doesn't reflect your policy, and may raise copyright and accuracy issues.

questions.stem: A report summary will be read aloud by a text-to-speech system. Which instruction is most likely to produce suitable output?
options: Don't use bullets, tables, or symbols.
Write in short, flowing spoken-style paragraphs without symbols or lists, because this will be read aloud by a text-to-speech system.
NEVER EVER use formatting.
Format the summary as you normally would.
questions.explanation: Positive instructions plus a reason work best. Knowing the output will be read aloud lets Claude handle cases the rule didn't spell out, such as abbreviations and numbers.
rationales: It says what to avoid but not what to do, and gives no reason.
Correct. It's a positive instruction with the reason behind it.
Shouting doesn't add clarity or the reason for the rule.
Normal formatting likely includes lists and symbols that read badly aloud.

questions.stem: Using the AI Fluency framework, which activity is the best example of DELEGATION?
options: Checking Claude's draft against the source policy for accuracy
Writing a detailed prompt describing the desired tone and format
Disclosing to readers that a report was prepared with AI assistance
Deciding that Claude will draft the first version of the training guide while you decide which policy positions to take
questions.explanation: Delegation is deciding whether, what, and how much of the work to hand to AI, while keeping the judgment-heavy parts with the human.
rationales: That is Discernment: evaluating output.
That is Description: communicating what you want.
That is part of Diligence: transparency and responsibility.
Correct. Dividing work between human and AI is Delegation.

questions.stem: After six rounds of revisions, a chat about a pricing proposal has drifted: it's built on a discount assumption you later rejected, and Claude keeps reintroducing it. What should you do? (Select two.)
options: Keep correcting the assumption in each new message
Ask Claude for a concise summary of the decisions you actually agreed on, excluding the rejected discount assumption
Switch to a lighter model to reduce confusion
Start a new chat with a consolidated prompt that includes the corrected assumptions and the agreed decisions
questions.explanation: When a thread is polluted by a rejected assumption, summarize the valid decisions and start fresh with a clean, consolidated prompt. That removes the rejected context Claude keeps picking up.
rationales: The rejected assumption stays in the thread's context, so it keeps resurfacing.
Correct. A clean summary captures what's still valid.
Model size isn't the cause. The polluted context is.
Correct. A fresh chat with corrected context stops the old assumption from influencing output.

questions.stem: You need Claude to recommend which of three CRM rollout plans to pursue. Which prompt addition most improves the quality of its recommendation?
options: Ask Claude to compare each plan against cost, risk, adoption effort, and time-to-value before giving a recommendation with its reasoning
Ask Claude to answer in one word so it's decisive
Ask Claude to pick the plan most companies choose
Ask Claude to recommend whichever plan is listed first
questions.explanation: Asking Claude to reason through explicit criteria before concluding produces a more thoughtful, inspectable recommendation.
rationales: Correct. Explicit criteria and visible reasoning improve quality and let you check the logic.
A one-word answer hides the reasoning and invites shallow judgment.
Popularity isn't a decision criterion for your context, and Claude may not know it reliably.
That's arbitrary and ignores the analysis entirely.

questions.stem: Which elements belong in a well-specified prompt for a customer-facing apology email about a service outage? (Select three.)
options: The audience and desired tone (e.g., affected enterprise customers; accountable, non-defensive)
A request that Claude invent a plausible root cause if none is known yet
What happened and what is being done to fix it, using confirmed facts you provide
An instruction to promise a full refund to make customers happy
Constraints such as length, and commitments the company has approved (and must not exceed)
questions.explanation: Good prompts supply verified facts, the audience and tone, and constraints, including which commitments are approved. Inventing causes or unapproved promises creates legal and trust risk.
rationales: Correct. Audience and tone shape an apology's effectiveness.
Inventing a root cause is fabrication and can mislead customers.
Correct. Confirmed facts ground the email.
Unapproved commitments create financial and legal exposure.
Correct. Limits and approved commitments prevent overpromising.

questions.stem: Claude's market summary includes a statistic: "68% of mid-market firms adopted AI in 2025," with no source. The summary will go to a client. What should you do?
options: Ask Claude "Are you sure?" and keep the statistic if it says yes
Keep it, because the number sounds reasonable
Round it to "about two-thirds" so it's less specific
Find and verify a primary source for the statistic, or remove it
questions.explanation: Specific statistics without sources are a common hallucination risk. Client-facing content needs verification against a primary source.
rationales: Self-confirmation isn't verification. Claude can confidently confirm a wrong number.
Sounding plausible is exactly why hallucinated statistics are dangerous.
Rounding an unverified number still presents it as fact.
Correct. Verify against a primary source, or remove the claim.

questions.stem: You use web search to research a regulatory change, and Claude's answer includes citations. What is the correct way to treat the result?
options: Open the cited sources and confirm they exist and actually support each key claim, especially claims without citations
Treat every sentence as verified because web search was enabled
Trust it if there are at least three citations
Re-run the same search and accept the answer if it matches
questions.explanation: Citations help, but a citation must actually support the specific claim, and not every sentence may be sourced. You still need to read the sources for high-stakes topics.
rationales: Correct. Confirm that the sources exist and support the claims.
Web search doesn't guarantee every statement is sourced or correctly interpreted.
The number of citations doesn't measure accuracy.
Consistency between runs isn't the same as correctness.

questions.stem: You uploaded a 5,000-row sales export and Claude reports total revenue by region. The numbers will go into a board pack. What's the most reliable way to validate them?
options: Ask Claude to double-check the totals in its head
Compare the totals with last quarter's to see whether they look similar
Have Claude compute the totals with code execution on the file, and reconcile key totals against your own spreadsheet calculation
Accept the totals if the percentages add up to 100%
questions.explanation: Real computation (code execution) is far more reliable than mental arithmetic over large data. Reconciling against an independent calculation provides verification.
rationales: Mental arithmetic over thousands of rows is error-prone. Repeating it doesn't make it more reliable.
Looking similar to last quarter doesn't validate this quarter's figures.
Correct. Real computation plus independent reconciliation.
Percentages can add up to 100% even when the underlying totals are wrong.

questions.stem: You want a summary of a 40-page vendor contract that you can trust for an internal decision. Which prompt technique most improves traceability?
options: Ask for the summary in the most concise form possible
Ask Claude to provide a supporting quote and section reference for each key point, and to say "not stated" when the contract is silent
Ask Claude to summarize from its general knowledge of vendor contracts
Ask for the summary in a table
questions.explanation: Requiring supporting quotes ties each claim to the source, and permitting 'not stated' discourages filling gaps with invented content.
rationales: Concise output can be less traceable, not more.
Correct. Quotes, section references, and permission to be uncertain make claims checkable.
General knowledge isn't this contract, which invites hallucination.
Format alone doesn't make claims traceable to the source.

questions.stem: Claude drafted a competitive analysis in a long conversation. You want an unbiased critique before sharing it with leadership. What's the best approach?
options: Ask the same conversation, "Is this analysis correct?"
Ask Claude in the same chat to rate its analysis from 1 to 10
Ask Claude to add more detail so it looks more thorough
Paste the draft into a new chat and ask Claude to critique it as a skeptical executive, listing weak claims and missing evidence
questions.explanation: A fresh chat isn't anchored on the original conversation's assumptions, and a skeptical reviewer framing draws out weaknesses. You should still verify key claims yourself.
rationales: The original thread tends to defend its own reasoning.
Self-rating in the same context is anchored and uninformative.
More detail doesn't mean more accuracy.
Correct. Independent context plus a critical framing.

questions.stem: Which type of content carries the HIGHEST hallucination risk and therefore needs the most careful verification?
options: Brainstormed names for an internal team offsite
A rewrite of your own paragraph for clarity
Specific legal citations and case references in a memo for a client
A list of generic tips for running better meetings
questions.explanation: Specific citations and references, especially in legal or regulated contexts, are high-risk for fabrication and high-stakes if they're wrong.
rationales: Brainstorms are low-stakes and creative by nature.
Rewriting your own content is grounded in text you provided.
Correct. Citations in client legal work are high-risk and high-stakes.
Generic tips are low-stakes and easy to sanity-check.

questions.stem: Claude helped draft interview evaluation criteria. Which review step best addresses fairness risk?
options: Check that the criteria are job-related, applied consistently to all candidates, and free of proxies for protected characteristics, with HR or legal review
Make sure the criteria are written in a friendly tone
Ask Claude whether the criteria are biased and accept its answer
Shorten the criteria so they're easier to apply
questions.explanation: Fairness review means confirming job-relatedness and consistency, and removing proxies for protected characteristics, with accountable human experts involved.
rationales: Correct. Substantive fairness checks with expert human review.
Tone doesn't address bias.
Claude's self-assessment isn't sufficient for a fairness review.
Brevity doesn't address fairness.

questions.stem: Claude's summary of a customer research report says "customers overwhelmingly want a mobile app." The report says 12 of 40 interviewees mentioned mobile. What kind of error is this?
options: A formatting error
Overreach: the summary overstates what the source supports
A tone mismatch
A calculation error caused by rounding
questions.explanation: Overreach is when a summary claims more than the source supports. 12 of 40 (30%) isn't 'overwhelming.'
rationales: Formatting isn't the issue. The substance is.
Correct. The conclusion goes beyond the evidence.
Tone isn't the core issue. The claim misrepresents the data.
No rounding was involved. It's a mischaracterization.

questions.stem: You'll publish a customer-facing whitepaper drafted with Claude. Which verification steps are appropriate for this level of stakes? (Select three.)
options: Rely on Claude's statement that the content is accurate
Verify every factual claim and statistic against primary sources
Skip review if the writing quality is high
Have a subject-matter expert review technical accuracy
Check that any quotes and references exist and are attributed correctly
questions.explanation: High-stakes external content needs full fact verification, expert review, and checks on quotes and references. Polished writing and AI self-assurance aren't evidence of accuracy.
rationales: Self-assurance isn't verification.
Correct. External claims need primary-source verification.
Fluent writing can hide factual errors.
Correct. Expert review catches subtle technical errors.
Correct. Quotes and references are a common fabrication risk.

questions.stem: You give Claude a rubric (accuracy, completeness, audience fit, format, risk) and ask it to self-review a draft before you read it. How should you treat its self-review?
options: As final approval, so no human review is needed
As useless, so you should never ask for self-review
As a substitute for checking facts against sources
As a helpful first pass that catches some issues, followed by your own review against the rubric and sources
questions.explanation: Self-review against a rubric can catch obvious gaps, but it doesn't replace human judgment and source verification.
rationales: Self-review isn't independent approval.
It's useful as a first pass. Dismissing it entirely wastes a cheap check.
It can't verify facts that need external sources.
Correct. Use it as a first pass, then review it yourself.

questions.stem: You ask Claude about a policy change your company announced yesterday, without providing any documents or enabling search. Claude answers in detail. What's the biggest concern?
options: Claude probably has no reliable knowledge of yesterday's internal announcement, so the details may be fabricated
The answer may be too long
Claude may use the wrong tone
The answer may use bullet points
questions.explanation: Claude can't know recent internal information unless you provide it or connect a source. Detailed answers about unknown facts are a classic hallucination pattern.
rationales: Correct. Without grounding, the details aren't trustworthy.
Length is a minor issue compared with accuracy.
Tone is secondary to whether the facts are real.
Formatting isn't the core risk.

questions.stem: A support agent uses Claude to draft a reply, and the draft says a premium customer is "eligible for a 60-day refund window." Policy says 30 days. What's the best process fix to prevent this kind of error?
